questions.stem: A test calls compute(data) once between two System.nanoTime() readings and reports the difference. What does that number mostly measure?

options.text: Interpreter and compiler work, not the hot code the JIT makes later.
options.says: A method starts in the interpreter and is compiled only after enough calls, so a single cold call does not show steady-state speed; warm-up or JMH is needed.

options.text: The fully optimised C2 code, since HotSpot compiles compute before its first run.
options.says: HotSpot compiles a method only after it crosses a call-count threshold; before that it is interpreted.

options.text: Mostly garbage collection, since the first call of compute triggers a collection.
options.says: A first call does not trigger a collection; the cost of a cold call comes from interpretation and compilation.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

questions.stem: Which method's Point allocation can the JIT remove entirely with escape analysis?

options.text: createPoint(x, y), which builds a new Point and returns it to its caller.
options.says: A returned object escapes the method (GlobalEscape), so it must be allocated on the heap.

options.text: printPoint(x, y), which builds a new Point and passes it to System.out.println.
options.says: Passing the object to println lets it escape into code the JIT must assume can keep it, so the allocation stays.

options.text: sumCoordinates(x, y), which builds a new Point and returns p.x() + p.y().
options.says: The Point never leaves the method (NoEscape), so scalar replacement turns its fields into locals and the allocation disappears.
